transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um… I’m not trying to make a big deal out of it, but things at work have been feeling pretty off.

Ever since I got that county safety award, some people at work have been… I don’t know, twisting my inspection reports, or asking these pointed budget questions like they’re trying to make me look crooked. My supervisor says it’s just normal review, and I’m trying to be reasonable about that, but it really doesn’t feel normal to me. It feels coordinated, like there’s an effort to discredit me.

I just thought maybe I should talk to someone before it gets… bigger, I guess.
How long has this feeling of being targeted or discredited at work been going on?

Um… I’d say about a year now. It kind of started after I got recognized for that county safety initiative. I mean, I don’t want to sound like I’m overconnecting things, but that’s when I really started noticing it.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear, or seen things that others didn't see, during this past year?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I hear normal stuff at work—radios, people talking, trucks backing up—but not voices that nobody else hears or anything like that.

And I haven’t seen things that weren’t there, as far as I know. I’m not trying to be difficult, I just… that’s not really what this has been about for me.
Aside from what's happening at work, do you find yourself generally distrustful or suspicious of people in other parts of your life, like family, friends, or people you meet socially?

Not really, no… I mean, I try not to be a suspicious person in general. With my family or friends, I don’t walk around thinking people are against me or anything like that.

It’s mostly work. Since that safety award, it’s just felt like certain people there started treating my reports differently, asking these budget questions in a way that feels pointed, like they’re trying to make me look dishonest. My supervisor says it’s normal review, and I’m trying to take that seriously, but… I don’t know. It feels coordinated to me.

I know that probably sounds strong. I’m just trying to explain it the way it feels.

Has this situation at work affected your ability to function in other areas, like your daily routine, relationships, or self-care, or are you managing those parts of your life as well as you always have?

I think I’m managing those parts okay, yeah. I mean, I still get to work on time, I do my inspections, I keep up with church, and I take care of myself—showering, eating, all that.

It’s mostly when those reports come up, or someone starts questioning what I spent money on, that I get… I don’t know, more tense. That’s where it causes problems. But day-to-day, I’d like to think I’m holding things together pretty well.
Have you noticed any changes in your motivation, emotional expression, or interest in activities you used to enjoy over this past year?

I don’t think so, not in any big way. I still do the things I normally do. I mean, maybe I’ve been a little more preoccupied or stressed at times, but I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in everything or stopped caring.

As far as emotions go, I think I’m about the same. I’m not trying to make it sound better than it is, but… I haven’t noticed some major change like that. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Have you or others noticed any times when your thoughts felt jumbled or hard to follow, or when you had trouble organizing your speech or actions?

No, I don’t think so. At least nobody’s told me that I’m not making sense or anything like that.

Sometimes I might get a little worked up when I’m trying to explain the work situation, and maybe I repeat myself because I want to be clear, but I wouldn’t say my thoughts are jumbled. I’m able to do my job and keep my day organized.

Does that answer what you’re asking?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (persecutory/conspiracy theme centered on coworkers discrediting him after receiving a safety award) persisting for approximately one year. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or thought, no negative symptoms, and no mood episode symptoms (mania or depression) accompanying the delusion. Functioning is preserved across domains—work performance, self-care, social/religious activities—except for situational distress triggered by the delusional content. The suspiciousness is circumscribed to the workplace context and does not generalize to other relationships, consistent with a single, encapsulated delusional system rather than the broader psychotic disorganization seen in schizophrenia or a mood disorder with psychotic features. This presentation, with duration >1 month, absence of schizophrenia's characteristic symptoms, and preserved psychosocial functioning outside the delusion, meets criteria for Delusional Disorder (F22).
